title: Operating Systems, Kernel Boundaries & Hypervisor Architecture

paras: Original handwriting preserved unchanged; editorial corrections expanded into mechanisms, practical examples and verification steps.

blocks.h2: 1 · What an operating system actually contains
paras: Original idea: OS is the main software managing hardware resources; applications are user-specific; services and utilities run in the background; libraries and system files support both.

Precise model: An operating system is not only its kernel. A Linux distribution typically contains the Linux kernel, system libraries (such as glibc or musl), an init/service manager (often systemd), device-management tools, shells, utilities and optional graphical components. Applications may be user-facing or background services; a driver may execute in kernel space or user space, depending on the driver architecture.

Example: When an Nginx service receives an HTTPS request, Nginx is an application in user space, the TCP/IP stack and socket operations involve the kernel, the NIC driver interacts with network hardware, and systemd may supervise the Nginx process. The OS does not literally “manage everything”: firmware, hypervisors, hardware controllers and applications have their own responsibilities.
Verify: uname -r , ps -p 1 -o comm= , systemctl status nginx (when installed), lsmod , lspci -k .

blocks.h2: 2 · Common OS services and the real execution path
paras: Example: cat /var/log/app.log | grep ERROR involves process creation, pipe IPC, file descriptors, VFS, storage reads, memory mappings and scheduler decisions—multiple OS services cooperating.

blocks.h2: 3 · User space, kernel space and system calls
paras: Correction: “Kernel space does; user space asks” is a useful starting analogy, not a universal rule. User-space applications perform most computation directly on the CPU; the kernel is entered for privileged services, interrupts, exceptions and system calls. Userspace is not a separate CPU, and the kernel is not one giant ordinary user process.

Real example: A Python program computes sum(range(100000)) largely in user mode; opening a file crosses into kernel mode. A context switch between processes and a user-to-kernel mode transition are related but distinct events.
Verify: strace -e trace=openat,read,write cat /etc/hostname (if strace installed); inspect /proc/self/maps .

blocks.h2: 4 · Kernel architecture: monolithic is not “one large process”
paras: Original note: Linux has a monolithic kernel handling CPU, memory and drivers with a single large process.

Example: A userspace application invokes read() ; the kernel may execute VFS and filesystem code in that process's context, while separate kernel workers handle deferred work. The same kernel serves all ordinary processes in a Linux host.
Cross-link: This is essential for understanding containers: containers typically share the host Linux kernel but isolate selected resources with namespaces and cgroups.

blocks.h2: 5 · Hardware virtualization, guest OS and hypervisors
paras: Original idea: A hypervisor abstracts physical CPU, RAM, storage and networking so multiple VMs can run independently.

How it works: Each VM is presented virtual CPUs, guest physical memory, virtual devices and a virtual disk. The guest OS runs its own kernel. CPU virtualization uses processor support such as Intel VT-x or AMD-V; memory virtualization commonly uses second-level address translation (EPT/NPT); I/O may be emulated, paravirtualized (virtio) or passed through.

Example: A 16-core, 64-GB Linux server might host several KVM guests. Assigning 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM to a guest does not mean four physical cores are permanently dedicated; the host schedules vCPU threads. Overcommitment, NUMA locality, storage latency and ballooning affect performance.
Verify: lscpu | grep -i virtualization ; on a KVM host inspect virsh list --all and virsh dominfo <vm> .

Correction: “Type 1 always fastest; Type 2 always slower” is too absolute. Hardware acceleration, device virtualization, drivers, workload, scheduling and configuration dominate many practical results.

Real-world failure example: A single KVM host runs a billing VM. If its motherboard fails, the VM stops even though it was virtualized. With two or more properly configured hosts, quorum/fencing, replicated or shared storage and HA management, the VM may be restarted elsewhere. Restart is not zero-downtime: application recovery and storage consistency still matter.

AWS correction: An AWS Region is a geographic grouping of Availability Zones; an AZ is one or more discrete data centers with independent power/networking characteristics. An EC2 instance is a virtual server (or bare-metal option). A Region is not equivalent to a single hypervisor, and an AZ is not simply one data center.

Analogy only: Hypervisor = building's space allocator; cluster manager = campus-wide relocation coordinator; AZ = independently engineered site grouping. These are explanatory analogies, not technical identities.

blocks.h2: 8 · VM versus container, with a practical example
paras: Example: A KVM VM runs Ubuntu with its own kernel and an ext4 filesystem on a virtual disk. A Docker container inside that VM runs Nginx and shares the VM's kernel. Kubernetes schedules Pods onto nodes; it does not turn every container into a full VM.
Commands: docker inspect <container> to review namespace/network settings; lsns to inspect namespaces; systemd-cgls for cgroup hierarchy.

blocks.h2: 9 · Walkthrough: request from browser to SSD and back
paras: Why it matters: This one request connects the notes on OS services, scheduling, RAM, storage abstraction, networking and virtualization. In a VM there is another virtual-device/host layer; in a container the application usually uses the shared host kernel.

tables.h2: 2 · Common OS services and the real execution path
rows: Shell invokes execve() ; kernel loads executable mappings, creates execution context and schedules runnable threads. ./app is not simply “placed in RAM all at once”: demand paging is common.
Virtual memory mappings, page tables, page faults, reclamation and permissions. mmap() maps memory; allocation by malloc() also involves a user-space allocator.
VFS mediates openat() , read() , write() across ext4, XFS, NFS and other filesystems.
Applications call read/write/ioctl; kernel drivers and device queues communicate with devices, often via interrupts and DMA.
Pipes, Unix-domain sockets, shared memory, signals, message queues; permissions and synchronization matter.
Kernel scheduler decides which runnable thread receives CPU time; cgroups can limit CPU/memory/I/O resources.
System calls return error codes, kernel logs record selected events, hardware can report faults; not all failures are recoverable.
Credentials, permissions, capabilities, LSMs (SELinux/AppArmor), namespaces, seccomp and auditing.
VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen, Nutanix AHV. “Bare metal” describes placement/architecture, not an automatic guarantee of superior performance in every workload.
VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels Desktop: hosted virtualization products relying on a host OS.
KVM is implemented as Linux kernel virtualization infrastructure, commonly paired with QEMU. Calling it simply Type 1 or Type 2 can obscure its actual architecture.
Machine emulator/virtualizer that can use KVM acceleration. QEMU alone is not synonymous with a hypervisor in all modes.
OS-level container technology, not a conventional full-machine hypervisor.
Product family with OS-level virtualization and VM capabilities depending on product/version; not one universal hypervisor type.

tables.h2: 8 · VM versus container, with a practical example
rows: Namespaces, cgroups, filesystem layers and capabilities
Strong isolation boundary when correctly configured
Useful process isolation; kernel is a shared attack surface
Can run different guest OS kernels supported by virtualization stack
Native Linux containers need a Linux kernel; desktop tooling may use a hidden VM

tables.h2: 10 · Revision guide: source ideas and corrected formulations
rows: OS coordinates many hardware/software resources; firmware, applications, hypervisors and controllers retain distinct responsibilities.
Linux is a modular monolithic kernel executing in privileged contexts, not one ordinary process.
User programs execute directly on CPU and request privileged kernel services through syscalls.
Hypervisor runs VMs; HA and cluster management require additional components.
Performance depends on hardware acceleration, I/O paths, workload and configuration.
KVM is kernel virtualization infrastructure, QEMU emulates/virtualizes machines, and LXC provides OS-level containers.
